details:
**Temple doors open in war, closed in peace**
The gates of the shrine of Janus in the Roman Forum (the Janus Geminus) were kept open whenever Rome was at war and closed only in times of peace. Because Rome was almost always fighting somewhere, the doors were rarely shut; the shrine was traditionally said to have been built by King Numa Pompilius.

**Two faces**
Janus is shown with two faces looking in opposite directions, one toward the past and one toward the future. This fits his role as the god of beginnings, endings, transitions, gates and doorways.

**Namesake of January**
The first month of the Roman year, Ianuarius (January), is named after Janus as the god of beginnings.

**Hot springs against the Sabines**
When the Sabines under Titus Tatius attacked Rome to avenge the abduction of the Sabine women, the traitor Tarpeia had let them into the citadel. Janus made a jet of boiling, sulfurous water burst from the ground at a gate, driving the invaders back, and one explanation for keeping his temple open in wartime was so he could come out to help Rome again.

**Carna and Cardea**
The nymph Carna (called Crane in Ovid) tricked her suitors by sending them into a cave and running away. Janus, who could see behind him, caught her; afterwards he made her Cardea, goddess of door hinges, and gave her a hawthorn branch to keep evil away from doorways.

**Sheltering Saturn in Latium**
When Saturn was driven out of the heavens by Jupiter, Janus, then king of Latium, welcomed him. The two ruled together during the Golden Age, and Saturn taught the people agriculture.

**Camese (Camasene) and Tiberinus**
In one tradition Janus came to Latium from Thessaly and married Camese (Camasene), ruling the land with her. Their son Tiberinus drowned in the river Albula, which was renamed the Tiber after him.

**Juturna and Fontus**
Janus was also called the husband of the water nymph Juturna, and their son was Fontus (Fons), the god of springs and wells. Juturna had earlier been one of Jupiter's lovers, an affair the nymph Lara revealed to Juno.

**Ovid's Fasti, Book 1**
Ovid's unfinished poem on the Roman calendar opens with an interview with Janus himself. He explains his two faces, why he receives the first offerings of incense and wine, why one side of the bronze as coin shows a ship, and the stories of Saturn and the Sabine attack.

**No Greek equivalent**
Unlike most major Roman gods, Janus has no counterpart in the Greek pantheon. The Etruscan god Culsans, a two-faced guardian of doorways, is often compared to him.

**First to be invoked in prayers**
In Roman ritual, Janus was called on first at the start of prayers and sacrifices, while Vesta was invoked last. He was also honored with the title "pater" (father), and the opening verses of the Carmen Saliare, the hymn of the Salian priests, were addressed to him.

**Key and staff**
Janus was often shown holding a key, as the god of doors, and a staff, the symbol of a doorkeeper or guide.

**Inventor of coins**
Janus was said to be the first to mint coins, and Roman bronze coins (the as) carried his two-faced head on one side and the prow of a ship on the other. He was also credited with teaching law and civilization.

**Epithets: Geminus, Matutinus, Consivius**
Janus had many surnames, including Geminus ("twin," for his double face), Matutinus (god of the morning) and Consivius ("the sower").

**Ianiculum and the Argiletum**
The Janiculum hill across the Tiber was said to be named after Janus, who ruled from a settlement there. His shrine in the Forum stood near the Argiletum, a street whose gate was linked to him.
